blockers.quote: The viewer's guess: the people with AI learned more.
blockers.why: Straw man misconception. After five acts showing students failing exams, mass layoffs, worker deskilling, and water plant staff unable to read a manual, no viewer believes programmers using AI learned more. The actual misconception the viewer holds by minute 8 is that using AI inevitably makes you dumber or destroys skills, which c15 and c16 break by demonstrating that outcome depends entirely on cognitive engagement versus passive handoff.
blockers.fix: Stage the genuine misconception: 'The viewer's guess: using AI inevitably destroys your skills.' Then flip it with the findings of c15 and c16: deskilling only occurred among those who handed over the coding (under 40%), whereas those who used AI to explain concepts scored 65% or more, preserving learning alongside the non-AI group's 67%.

keep.quote: Then the monthly exams. Closed book. No AI in the room. Within six months, down 20 percent, against their own old average (c06).
Homework done in forty-five minutes instead of sixty-four (c05).

A group of researchers argue this is the real risk. No robot army. No evil machine. A slow handover of one small decision at a time, until people aren't steering (c13). They argue it; nobody has measured it.
